bullets.text: Ryo Lu's ryOS frames AI as a playful creative instrument, not merely a productivity tool.
The opening shifts attention from generated junk to the human choices behind it.
New media repeatedly bring cheap output, public anxiety, and a slower development of taste.
The essay sees AI's difference chiefly in scale and speed, not inevitable disposability.
Depth requires direction and judgment; a vague prompt cannot supply either on its own.
Taste means understanding the tool, setting constraints, and deliberately shaping the interaction.
Calibration repeatedly adjusts questions, prompts, and constraints rather than accepting the first result.
The model provides structure; human persistence and judgment give the work substance.
Blaming the model can obscure the standards people and platforms reward.
The essay links slop's spread to incentives favoring engagement and speed over originality.
Printing, desktop publishing, and video illustrate the argument that useful filters develop over time.
Faster production makes deliberate refinement more important, not less.
Stewardship means slowing down enough to shape the tool around what people value.
The conclusion puts responsibility for standards and curation back in human hands.

notes.text: The opening's standard of success is soul and originality, not throughput. Keep that distinction in view when the argument turns from a playful experiment to mass-produced slop.
If depth depends on intent and taste, what would a better input process look like before the first prompt is written? The discussion of constraints offers one starting point.
Calibration is presented as repeated judgment, not a single clever prompt. The craft lies in editing the interaction as well as evaluating what comes out of it.
Who is rewarded for speed over originality: the user, the publisher, or the platform? This passage broadens the responsibility question beyond the person typing a prompt.
The closing offers responsibility rather than reassurance: better tools still require human standards. Curation and refinement, rather than withdrawal, are the proposed response.
